title: Silence, Prayers, and Four Trumpets
overview: After a hush in heaven, the prayers of God's people rise like incense, and four trumpet blasts bring limited disasters on land, sea, fresh water and sky as a warning of worse to come.

parts.label: Silence in heaven (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The seventh seal is opened, the last of the seals whose opening began in chapter 6, and heaven goes completely quiet; scholars are unsure why, though awe or tense expectation are common readings. Seven angels who stand before God are then given trumpets, which in Israel sounded alarms and called people to battle.

parts.label: Prayers rise like incense (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: An angel burns incense on heaven's golden altar, modeled on the incense altar in the temple, and its smoke rises to God along with the prayers of God's people. Readers differ on this angel: some Protestants see Jesus acting as priest, others an ordinary angel serving, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians often point to it as angels helping bring prayers to God.

parts.label: Fire hurled to earth (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: The angel fills the same fire pan with coals from the altar and throws it to earth, bringing thunder, lightning and an earthquake. Many readers connect this to the cry for justice from persecuted believers in 6:10, so the prayers seem to be answered with judgment as the trumpet angels get ready.

parts.label: Land and sea struck (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: The first trumpet brings hail and fire mixed with blood that burn part of the land and trees and all the grass, and the second sends a blazing mass like a mountain into the sea, killing sea creatures and wrecking ships. These echo the plagues on Egypt in Exodus, and the repeated limit to one third is widely read as harm that is severe but held back from being total.

parts.label: Bitter water, darkened sky (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: The third trumpet brings a falling star named Wormwood, after a very bitter plant the prophets used as a picture of suffering, and the text says plainly that many people die from the poisoned water. The fourth darkens part of the sun, moon and stars, like Egypt's plague of darkness, and readers debate whether these are literal events or pictures of a world thrown into disorder.

parts.label: The eagle's three woes (v. 13)
parts.note: An eagle flying high overhead, where everyone can see it, cries woe three times as a warning that the last three trumpets will be worse still. Some older English versions say angel here because they followed later Greek copies, while the oldest copies say eagle.

disagreement: Christians differ on what these trumpets describe: some read them as events in the first century Roman world, some as a timeline of later history such as the fall of Rome, some as disasters still to come before Jesus returns, and others as symbolic pictures of judgment that recur throughout history.
think: When you have wanted a wrong to be put right, what did you actually hope would happen?
